questions.question: What is a functional interface in Java?
questions.title: Functional Interface in Java 8
questions.direct_answer: A **functional interface** has exactly **one abstract method** (SAM — Single Abstract Method). It can have multiple default and static methods. The `@FunctionalInterface` annotation verifies this at compile time. Functional interfaces are the target type for lambda expressions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Foundational Java 8 knowledge — functional interfaces are the contract for lambdas
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking @FunctionalInterface creates the constraint — the annotation only validates it
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the four key built-in functional interfaces: Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier

sections.title: Built-in Functional Interfaces in java.util.function
sections.content:
- **Predicate<T>** — T → boolean: used for filtering
- **Function<T,R>** — T → R: used for mapping/transformation
- **Consumer<T>** — T → void: used for side effects (forEach)
- **Supplier<T>** — () → T: used for lazy value creation
- **BiFunction<T,U,R>** — (T,U) → R: function with two inputs
- **UnaryOperator<T>** — T → T: special Function where input = output type
- **BinaryOperator<T>** — (T,T) → T: two same-type inputs, same type output

sections.title: Functional Interface Examples
How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method. That single method is what a lambda implements. The @FunctionalInterface annotation is optional but recommended — it makes the compiler verify that you only have one abstract method. Java 8 added a whole package of built-in functional interfaces in java.util.function. The four you absolutely need to know are: Predicate which takes a value and returns boolean — used for filtering. Function which takes a value and returns another — used for mapping. Consumer which takes a value and returns nothing — used for side effects like printing. And Supplier which takes nothing and returns a value — used for lazy initialization.

beats.text: A functional interface is an interface with exactly one abstract method — sometimes called a SAM, which stands for Single Abstract Method. That one method is what a lambda implements. The interface can also have default and static methods — those don't count against the one-abstract-method rule.

The @FunctionalInterface annotation is optional. It tells the compiler to verify that the interface really does have only one abstract method. If someone adds a second abstract method by mistake, the annotation causes a compile error. It's basically a safety net.

items: Predicate takes a value and returns boolean — used in stream filter()
Function takes a value and returns a different value — used in stream map()
Consumer takes a value and returns nothing — used in stream forEach()
Supplier takes nothing and returns a value — used in Optional.orElseGet()

beats.text: candidates miss: the @FunctionalInterface annotation does NOT create the functional interface — any interface with one abstract method is already functional. The annotation just validates it. Runnable has been a functional interface since Java 1 — it just didn't get the annotation until Java 8.

questions.question: What is the difference between Predicate, Function, Consumer, and Supplier?
questions.title: Predicate vs Function vs Consumer vs Supplier
questions.direct_answer: **Predicate<T>**: T → boolean (test/filter). **Function<T,R>**: T → R (transform). **Consumer<T>**: T → void (side effect). **Supplier<T>**: () → T (produce). These four cover the four fundamental patterns of what a function can do.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can name and distinguish the four key functional interfaces
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing Function and Consumer — Function returns something, Consumer does not
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete real-world use case for each from Stream operations

sections.title: Four Key Functional Interfaces
sections.content:
| Interface | Signature | Returns | Stream Use | Example |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Predicate<T> | T → boolean | boolean | filter() | s -> s.length() > 3 |
| Function<T,R> | T → R | R | map() | String::length |
| Consumer<T> | T → void | nothing | forEach() | System.out::println |
| Supplier<T> | () → T | T | generate(), Optional.orElseGet() | ArrayList::new |

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: The four key functional interfaces cover the four things a function can do. Predicate tests a value and returns true or false — it's used in stream's filter(). Function transforms a value into a different type — used in stream's map(). Consumer takes a value and does something with it without returning anything — used in forEach(). Supplier produces a value without taking any input — used in Optional.orElseGet() for lazy computation. If you can connect each one to its stream operation, that shows you really understand how they work together.

questions.question: What is @FunctionalInterface annotation and is it required?
questions.title: @FunctionalInterface Annotation in Java
questions.direct_answer: `@FunctionalInterface` is an optional annotation that tells the **compiler to verify** the interface has exactly one abstract method. It is NOT required — any interface with one abstract method can be used as a functional interface. The annotation just prevents accidental addition of a second abstract method.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding that @FunctionalInterface is optional but recommended
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking an interface MUST have @FunctionalInterface to be used as a lambda target
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Runnable and Callable work as functional interfaces without @FunctionalInterface on them

sections.title: @FunctionalInterface Usage
How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: @FunctionalInterface is an informational annotation — it tells the compiler to check that your interface has exactly one abstract method. If someone adds a second abstract method by mistake, the compiler flags an error. But it's not required. Runnable and Comparable don't have @FunctionalInterface but they still work as lambda targets. The annotation is basically defensive programming for interface designers. I always add it when creating a custom functional interface because it documents intent and prevents accidental breakage.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app using Java 8 streams and lambdas
speakable_v2.hook: A lot of freshers think you must put @FunctionalInterface on an interface before using it as a lambda target. That's not true — here's what the annotation actually does.

beats.text: @FunctionalInterface is a compile-time validation annotation. It tells the compiler to verify that the interface has exactly one abstract method. If someone accidentally adds a second abstract method to the interface, the compiler flags an error right away.

It's not required. Any interface with exactly one abstract method is already a functional interface — the annotation just validates that. Runnable has been a valid lambda target since Java 8 even though it doesn't have @FunctionalInterface on it.

Best practice: always add @FunctionalInterface when you're designing an interface to be used as a lambda target. It documents your intent clearly and protects against accidental breakage if someone later adds a method to the interface.

gotcha: if you put @FunctionalInterface on an interface that has two abstract methods, you get a compile error on the annotation line itself — not on the method that was added. This is how you'd know someone broke a functional interface contract.

speakable_v2.cap: @FunctionalInterface is optional — it validates your design but doesn't create anything. Any single-abstract-method interface works as a lambda target regardless.

questions.question: How do you compose two Predicates in Java 8?
questions.title: Composing Predicates in Java 8
questions.direct_answer: `Predicate` has **default methods** `and()`, `or()`, and `negate()` for composition. `p1.and(p2)` creates a new Predicate that is true only when both are true. `p1.or(p2)` is true when either is true. `p.negate()` inverts the Predicate.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Java 8 Predicate composition — shows real usage beyond just definitions
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using && inside a lambda instead of and() method — works but misses the composition approach
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how composed predicates make stream filters more readable and reusable

sections.title: Predicate Composition
Key Points
sections.content:
- and() — logical AND of two predicates (both must be true)
- or() — logical OR (either must be true)
- negate() — logical NOT (inverts the predicate)
- Predicate.not(p) — static method (Java 11+) for negating without a variable
- Composition makes predicates reusable — define once, combine as needed
- Function also supports composition: andThen() and compose()

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Predicate has three default methods for composition: and(), or(), and negate(). You create individual predicates and combine them. So notEmpty.and(longEnough) gives you a new predicate that's only true when both conditions are met. This is more reusable than writing the combined logic inline — you can mix and match predicates in different ways. For negation, Predicate has a negate() method, and Java 11 added a static Predicate.not() method which is more readable in stream filter chains.

followup_questions: What is the difference between Predicate.and() and writing && in a lambda?
How does Function.andThen() work?

seo.metaTitle: Predicate Composition Java 8 | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: How to compose Predicates in Java 8 using and(), or(), negate()? Reusable predicate combination for stream filter operations.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app using Java 8 streams and lambdas
speakable_v2.hook: Instead of cramming all your filter conditions into one lambda, you can compose separate Predicates — and that makes them reusable across your whole codebase.

items: and() — both predicates must return true, short-circuits on first false
or() — either predicate must return true, short-circuits on first true
negate() — inverts the predicate, true becomes false and vice versa

beats.text: You define each condition as its own Predicate, then combine them. notEmpty.and(longEnough) gives a new Predicate that's only true when both hold. You can chain as many as you need. The composed predicate is just another Predicate — pass it anywhere a Predicate is expected.

The real benefit is reuse. Define a notEmpty Predicate once. Define a startsWithA Predicate once. Combine them differently in different parts of your code. Versus embedding the full inline lambda everywhere — that's duplication.

non-obvious: Predicate.and() is not the same as writing and-and inside a lambda. Both work, but and() creates a composed Predicate object you can store, reuse, and test in isolation. The inline lambda is a one-off that you can't reuse without copying.

speakable_v2.cap: Predicate.and(), or(), and negate() let you build complex filter conditions from simple reusable parts rather than cramming everything into one lambda.

questions.question: What is Function.andThen() vs Function.compose() in Java?
questions.title: Function.andThen() vs Function.compose()
questions.direct_answer: `f.andThen(g)` means: apply f first, then apply g to the result (f → g). `f.compose(g)` means: apply g first, then apply f to the result (g → f). `andThen` is more intuitive for left-to-right reading.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Function composition methods — shows depth of Java 8 knowledge
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Getting the order backwards for compose()
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show with types: f: A→B, g: B→C, f.andThen(g) gives A→C

sections.title: andThen vs compose
andThen vs compose
sections.content:
| Method | Order | Reads naturally |
|---|---|---|
| f.andThen(g) | f first, then g | Left-to-right |
| f.compose(g) | g first, then f | Right-to-left (mathematical order) |
| When to use | Pipeline building | Mathematical composition |

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: andThen and compose both chain two Functions, but in different orders. f.andThen(g) means: apply f, then apply g to the result — left-to-right, which is how you'd naturally read a pipeline. f.compose(g) means: apply g first, then f — which matches mathematical function composition notation but is less intuitive for most developers. In practice, andThen is much more commonly used because it reads naturally as a pipeline.

seo.metaTitle: Function andThen vs compose Java 8 | Java Interview Questions for Freshers
seo.metaDescription: Difference between Function.andThen() and Function.compose() in Java 8 — execution order, type alignment, and when to use each.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app using Java 8 streams and lambdas
speakable_v2.hook: andThen and compose do the same thing — chain two functions — but in opposite orders. Getting them mixed up gives you type errors that are hard to debug.

groups.heading: andThen
groups.text: f.andThen(g) means: run f first, then pass the result to g. This is left-to-right order — the same order you'd read a pipeline. Most developers find this natural. f is a String-to-Integer function, g is Integer-to-String, so f.andThen(g) gives you String-to-String.

groups.heading: compose
groups.text: f.compose(g) means: run g first, then pass the result to f. This is right-to-left order — it matches the mathematical notation for function composition. Less intuitive for most Java developers. In practice it's rarely used.

beats.text: gotcha: the types must align. If f goes from A to B, and g goes from B to C, then f.andThen(g) works and gives you A to C. But f.compose(g) would require g to go from A to A so that f can then process it. Mix up the order and the type checker catches you — but the error message isn't always obvious.

speakable_v2.cap: andThen is left-to-right and natural for pipelines; compose is right-to-left and mathematical — use andThen in practice.

questions.question: How do you create a custom functional interface in Java?
questions.title: Custom Functional Interface in Java
questions.direct_answer: Define an interface with **exactly one abstract method** and annotate it with `@FunctionalInterface`. Choose the method signature to match what your lambda will do. Custom functional interfaces are needed when none of the built-in ones (Predicate, Function, etc.) match your signature.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to create reusable functional interfaces for domain-specific operations
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Creating a custom functional interface when Function<T,R> or BiFunction would already work
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a practical example: a functional interface that throws checked exceptions

sections.title: Custom Functional Interface Examples
When to Create Custom Functional Interfaces
sections.content:
- When you need to throw a checked exception from a lambda
- When the built-in interfaces don't match (e.g., three input parameters)
- When you want a domain-specific name that documents intent (PasswordEncoder vs Function<String,String>)
- When you're building a library and want clear API contracts
- When you need specialized primitive versions for performance

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Creating a custom functional interface is straightforward — just define an interface with one abstract method and add @FunctionalInterface. The most practical reason to create one is when you need to throw a checked exception from your lambda. The built-in Function, Predicate, etc. don't declare throws, so you can't throw IOException inside them. Creating an IOFunction that extends Function but declares throws IOException solves this. Another reason is domain clarity — a PasswordEncoder interface with an encode method is more self-documenting than Function<String, String>.

questions.question: What are primitive functional interfaces like IntPredicate and LongFunction?
questions.title: Primitive Functional Interfaces in Java 8
questions.direct_answer: Java provides **specialized primitive functional interfaces** like `IntPredicate`, `IntFunction`, `ToIntFunction`, `LongConsumer` to avoid **autoboxing overhead**. When working with streams of primitives (`IntStream`, `LongStream`), these avoid wrapping primitives in Integer/Long objects.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of performance considerations in Java 8 functional programming
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using Function<Integer, Integer> when IntUnaryOperator would avoid boxing
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the autoboxing cost and how primitive streams (IntStream) use these automatically

sections.title: Primitive Functional Interfaces
sections.content:
Autoboxing (int → Integer, long → Long) has a cost: object allocation and cache misses. For performance-sensitive code with large datasets:

- `IntPredicate` — int → boolean (instead of Predicate<Integer>)
- `IntFunction<R>` — int → R
- `ToIntFunction<T>` — T → int
- `IntUnaryOperator` — int → int
- `IntBinaryOperator` — (int, int) → int

Similar families exist for long and double.

When you use `IntStream.filter()`, `IntStream.map()`, etc., these interfaces are used internally, avoiding boxing for the entire pipeline.

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Java provides primitive-specialized functional interfaces to avoid autoboxing overhead. When you write Function<Integer, Integer>, every int value gets boxed into an Integer object — extra allocation and GC pressure. IntUnaryOperator does the same logical thing but works with raw ints throughout. This matters when processing large collections of numbers. When you use IntStream instead of Stream<Integer>, all the operations — filter, map, reduce — use these primitive interfaces automatically. For most business logic with small datasets, the difference is negligible, but for numerical processing it can be significant.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app using Java 8 streams and lambdas
speakable_v2.hook: When you use Function of Integer to Integer with a million numbers, you're boxing every single int into an object. Primitive functional interfaces eliminate that entirely.

beats.text: Every time you use Function of Integer to Integer, each primitive int gets wrapped in an Integer object. That's object allocation and garbage collection pressure for every element in your pipeline. With a small list it doesn't matter. With millions of numbers it adds up.

Java provides primitive-specialized versions of all the main functional interfaces. IntPredicate is int to boolean — no boxing. IntUnaryOperator is int to int — no boxing. ToIntFunction takes a T and returns a plain int. The whole family exists for int, long, and double.

When you use IntStream instead of Stream of Integer, all the operations automatically use these primitive interfaces internally. So just choosing IntStream over Stream gets you the performance benefit without having to think about which primitive interface to pick.

non-obvious: for a typical web application processing a list of 50 users, the boxing overhead is invisible. Primitive interfaces matter for batch processing, numerical algorithms, or any pipeline with millions of elements. Don't prematurely optimize — profile first.

speakable_v2.cap: Primitive functional interfaces like IntPredicate and IntUnaryOperator eliminate autoboxing overhead — use them or IntStream when processing large volumes of numbers.
